Messages.Author: Eric Simon
Messages.Body:
I'll let Eric Chiang give the more detailed version, but at the small
Infernal Plague tourney in Evanston, I ran into something of a
quandary. Because there were only four players, we had opted for the
"three rounds, no final" option, and because of this I was in a
situation in which I had to choose between maximizing vps in a game or
maintaining the possibility of winning the tournament. Eric Chiang
had won round one, and in round two I was his predator. His prey
(John Flournoy) had taken one player out, leaving three of us, and I
was going down soon. Eric was close but seemed unlikely to be able to
take out John before John got me. I have Julia Prima and all the
stealth I need to swing this one way or the other (but not enough
bleed to take out Eric). Because I am scrupulously avoiding
considering out-of-game factors (like who already has a VP in the
tourney), I make a deal with Eric that he will withdraw after ousting
John if I bleed John right now. He agrees, and holds to the deal. I
get my VP (more than I would have otherwise) and Eric gets the second
game win. This of course renders the third round moot, as Eric has
locked out the tournament at this point.

So, I know that I did the "right thing" in that I didn't take into
account out-of-game considerations when deciding my play, and instead
maximized my VPs. But I also see the "right thing" as having been
fairly wrong in this case. Since we were not playing a final, two GWs
decided the tournament, and I basically made a deal trading the
tournament for a single VP. Now, John's deck was quite nasty and
swept the final round, so actually it would have given the tournament
to him, but still I would have had the CHANCE to win in the third
round.

My question is - can this issue be corrected for in the "three
rounds/no final" situation that is now tournament legal, and if so,
how?

Eric Simon
Prince of Chicago

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Eric Simon" <vol...@yahoo.com> wrote in
message news:6f81fa2c.04111...@posting.google.com...

(Story about having to decide between having a chance to win the tournament
vs. adhering strictly to the in-game motivation rule.)

> My question is - can this issue be corrected for in the "three
> rounds/no final" situation that is now tournament legal, and if so,
> how?

I don't understand the question. There is no difference, in this
sense, between 3R+0F vs. xR+F. The same situation may arise perfectly
well in a tournament WITH a final - just that you'd be aggravatging about
playing in a way that would get you a spot in the final vs. playing in a
way that would allow you to finish 1st in the standings after three
rounds. I think it may be a little more common in the no-finals type
tournament because everyone is angling for top spot ONLY in the preliminary
rounds than being OK finishing in one of the top 5 spots. But the quality
of the issue is no different.

Fred

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>My question is - can this issue be corrected for in the "three
>rounds/no final" situation that is now tournament legal, and if so,
>how?

Continuously playing against all of your competition was no help.

I'm constantly amazed by two things:
a) That people play more than one round when they only have enough players for
a single table. It's so much fairer to just play one game for all of the
marbles. So many of the problems associated with tournament play are
eliminated when you play only one game, for one thing.

b) That people think there's something wrong with tournament players playing
to win the tournament. Because rational play is play that leads to tournament
victory (well, technically, rational play factors in maximizing prizes, but
assuming common prize distributions ...), playing to win a game at the cost of
tournament chances is irrational.

BAH! (I've given Curevei grief about this before, he knows it well...)

...that people would prefer to play three rounds of tournament rather
than just one, whatever its flaws?

> b) That people think there's something wrong with tournament players playing
> to win the tournament. Because rational play is play that leads to
> tournament victory (well, technically, rational play factors in maximizing
> prizes, but assuming common prize distributions ...), playing to win a game
> at the cost of tournament chances is irrational.

I don't know that anyone thinks there's anything wrong with it. It's just
that those are tournament rules, for better or worse. I'm neutralish on it
myself, but I could probably argue from the perspective that thinks this is
bad: because it tends to warp games in the last preliminary round or so.

For instance, I once played a game in Los Angeles in the second round where
I was once AGAIN on the same table as Mike Curtois's $#&#! super-intercept
thug Tzimisce free repeating Horrid Form deck. Of course, I'd already been
its predator in the first round (as always, once per trip to LA) so I was
spared that experience again. But I knew there was no winning the game unless
it was defeated. Two of the other players at the table agreed with me and
were more than willing to gang up on him. The last guy, however, needed only
one victory point to make the finals (in his reckoning), so he sold out to
Mike to get his one victory point in exchange for any chance of winning the
game, and Mike won. Of course, he might have told this story a different
way, but it's at least very arguable that we might have gotten him to gang
up on Mike too had it been the first round or had he needed a game win to
make the finals.

Of course, that also demonstrates that it's hard to enforce the rule that
people must ignore such out-of-game considerations, but that's a different
issue.

Fred

This is true, but unhelpful in my particular case. LSJ has determined
that once you win, you can finish as you like. Also, if you can only
get a certain number of VPs (including 0), you can get that number
however you like. The choice that I had to make, however, was between
0 VPs and a chance to win the tournament and 1 VP with no chance to
win the tournament. By 5.2, I am not allowed to choose the first
option, since I am not pursuing the goal of the game. LSJ also points
out that I am not obligated to believe my opponent and make the deal
that I made, but that's kind of dishonest in spirit if not in letter.

I guess what I'm saying is that I have trouble with 5.2 as it is
currently worded because of all the grey area. Since everyone does it
anyway, would it really be a problem to allow people to consider
TOURNAMENT victory as well as game victory a legal goal?
